sources.title: Creator of TypeScript: 10x Faster Typescript, Why AI Won't Replace SWEs | Anders Hejlsberg
limitations: This is a publisher-hosted transcript of an interview, not an independent benchmark or a direct release note.
The transcript supports what Hejlsberg said at its stated timecodes; it does not establish that the same outcomes will hold for another codebase or team.

claims.text: Peterman's episode and transcript cover the TypeScript compiler's Go port, limited use of LLMs in that migration, tooling performance, and AI's effect on software engineering.
claims.notes: The episode page lists those subjects and timecoded sections.

claims.text: Hejlsberg says the team chose to port rather than rewrite the compiler in order to preserve semantics, algorithms, and behavior relied on for backward compatibility; Go fit their requirements for native code, garbage collection, and shared-memory concurrency.
claims.notes: Transcript 10:35-13:27. This records his account of the choice, not a universal language-selection rule.

claims.text: Hejlsberg says that for a large migration, using AI to build a transformation program can be preferable to letting AI translate the whole codebase directly, because the program can then produce the same transformation on every run and presents a smaller surface to validate.
claims.notes: Transcript 15:16-18:23. His statement is conditional and still assumes validation of the tool.

claims.text: Hejlsberg says AI agents can create many more code-writing workers and argues that a two-minute type-check delay after each generated change is unacceptable in a large project, making faster tooling more valuable.
claims.notes: Transcript 49:30-50:00. This is an expert's operating judgment and scenario, not a measured productivity study.

claims.text: When AI increases the number or frequency of code-producing attempts, validation-loop latency is more likely to constrain useful throughput; teams should measure that loop before treating agent count as the main scaling lever.
claims.notes: Editorial inference. A bounded Aaron-owned timing check executed 2026-08-24 (personal-proof.md in this package: aaronguoblog publishing-gate build; sequential pair 86 s vs concurrent pair 56 s wall with 33% per-attempt latency degradation at 2x parallelism on a mostly idle 18-core machine) is consistent with the inference in one local case. It still does not prove a general multiplier or a prescribed target duration.
